summary: Defines a MIME content type for message disposition notifications, which report what happened to a message after delivery, plus header fields to request them. It is an Internet Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: A read receipt for email in a machine-readable form.

questions: what is a message disposition notification
how do email read receipts work
can a read receipt be ignored
subtitle: How email can ask for, and report back, what a recipient's mail program did with a message.

tldr.problem: Internet Mail had no standard, machine-readable way for a sender to learn what happened to a message after delivery, such as whether it was displayed, deleted or processed, while still respecting recipients' privacy.
tldr.mechanism: A sender adds a Disposition-Notification-To header to ask for a receipt. The recipient's mail program may answer with a multipart/report message whose second part has the media type message/disposition-notification and lists fields such as Final-Recipient and Disposition.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8098 is an Internet Standard that obsoletes RFC 3798. The request is only a request: the recipient's program may ignore it, and an MDN is not proof the message was read.

today: RFC 8098 is an Internet Standard (STD 85). It obsoletes RFC 3798 and updates RFC 2046 and RFC 3461. The metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What an MDN Is For
sections.content:
A Message Disposition Notification (MDN) tells the sender of a message what happened to it after it was successfully delivered. The RFC names conditions such as the message being displayed, printed, deleted without display, or the recipient refusing to provide MDNs. This is the Internet Mail counterpart of the 'read receipts' found in X.400 and proprietary LAN-based systems.

The RFC lists several purposes. MDNs inform people of a message's fate in a way largely independent of human language, let mail user agents track what happened to messages they sent, and carry notifications to and from foreign mail systems through gateways. The format must be readable by humans and machine parsable, must let a sender tie an MDN to the original message and recipient even after forwarding, and must be extensible.

RFC 8098 defines the notification format and the header fields used to request one. It obsoletes RFC 3798 and updates RFC 2046 (handling of message/partial) and RFC 3461 (when the Original-Recipient header is generated).
sections.plainLanguage: Normally once you post a letter you never know what happened to it. An MDN is a note back that says what the person did with your letter.

sections.title: Requesting an MDN
sections.content:
A sender asks for notifications by putting a Disposition-Notification-To header field in the message, with one or more addresses to send them to. It may appear at most once. The RFC stresses that this is merely a request, and the recipient's user agent is always free to silently ignore it. Including a Message-ID is especially useful so the MDN can be matched to the original.

The consent rules are strict. The RFC strongly recommends that the user agent get the user's consent before sending an MDN, with the default being not to send. An MDN must not be sent automatically if the address in Disposition-Notification-To differs from the Return-Path address, if there is no Return-Path, or if there is more than one distinct address in the header. In those cases the user must confirm, and if that is not possible no MDN is sent. This limits mail loops and mail bombing.

Two optional companion headers exist. Disposition-Notification-Options carries extension parameters marked required or optional, though this RFC defines none. Original-Recipient records the address the sender originally wrote, taken from the ORCPT parameter in SMTP, so an MDN can be matched per recipient even after forwarding. A user agent must not issue more than one MDN per recipient, and an MDN must never be generated in response to an MDN.
sections.plainLanguage: You write 'please tell me when you open this' on the letter. The friend can say yes, no or ask you first, and they only get to send one answer.

sections.title: The Shape of an MDN
sections.content:
An MDN is a MIME message with the top-level type multipart/report (defined in RFC 6522) and the report-type disposition-notification. It has up to three parts. The first is a human-readable explanation. The second has the media type message/disposition-notification and holds the machine-readable fields. The third, optional, returns the original message or part of it; if the original was encrypted, it must come back in its original encrypted form.

Addressing follows tight rules. The MDN is addressed, in both the header and the transport envelope, to the addresses in the original Disposition-Notification-To field. Its From header holds the address of the person the notification is issued for. Its envelope sender must be null (<>), so that no delivery status notifications or other replies are produced in response. An MDN must not itself request an MDN, and its Message-ID must differ from that of the original. Each MDN describes exactly one message for exactly one recipient.

The second part must use 7bit encoding to remain readable by non-MIME mail readers. The media type registers the file extension .disposition-notification.
sections.plainLanguage: The reply is a small package with three pieces: a note a person can read, a form a computer can read, and sometimes a copy of the original letter.

sections.title: Fields in the Report Part
sections.content:
The body of the message/disposition-notification part is a list of fields written like email header fields. Final-Recipient and Disposition are required. The others are optional or conditional.

  • Reporting-UA names the mail program that generated the MDN. It should be sent unless configured otherwise, and should avoid needless detail that could fingerprint the user.
  • MDN-Gateway appears only when a gateway translated a foreign notification into an MDN.
  • Original-Recipient is included only if the original recipient address is reliably known.
  • Final-Recipient is the recipient the MDN is issued for. It may be an alias address rather than a private personal address.
  • Original-Message-ID must be present if and only if the original message had a Message-ID.
  • Error adds text when the error disposition modifier is used.

Addresses carry an address-type such as rfc822. Field names are case insensitive. New fields, modifiers and options must be registered with IANA under the 'Specification Required' policy. The RFC also points to RFC 6533 for MDNs that need non-ASCII text in these fields.
sections.plainLanguage: The form has boxes: who is answering, which letter this is about, and what they did with it. Some boxes are optional, and a few are only filled in in special cases.

sections.title: Disposition: What Happened and How
sections.content:
The Disposition field describes the action taken, in the form action-mode/sending-mode; disposition-type, optionally followed by modifiers.

The action mode is manual-action (the user explicitly did it) or automatic-action (for example generated by a delivery agent or a rule). The sending mode is MDN-sent-manually (the user approved this MDN) or MDN-sent-automatically (the program was preconfigured). To protect privacy, the manual forms must be the defaults for user agents.

There are four disposition types. displayed means the message was shown to someone reading the mailbox, with no guarantee it was read or understood. dispatched means it was sent somewhere, for example printed, faxed or forwarded, without necessarily being displayed. processed means a rule or server handled it without displaying it. deleted means it was deleted, and the user may undelete it later. The only modifier defined is error; others can be registered later, and an MDN with an unknown modifier must not trigger an error message to its sender.

Mailing lists get their own guidance: successful distribution to the list may be treated as final disposition, with the exploder sending a processed MDN, rather than passing the request on to subscribers.
sections.plainLanguage: The answer says what the friend did: looked at it, passed it on, filed it away unseen, or threw it out. It also says whether a person chose that or a machine did.

sections.title: Forgery, Privacy and Mail Bombing
sections.content:
The RFC is frank about the risks. MDNs can be forged as easily as ordinary mail, so they can report a disposition that never happened or arrive unsolicited. A spam or phishing message can include a Disposition-Notification-To header to trick the recipient into replying, so MDN processing should only be invoked once the message is verified as authentic.

Privacy is the central worry. An MDN can reveal when a message was read, in which mail client and on which operating system. Someone with access to the message stream could use the request to monitor a target's reading habits, which is why MDNs should not be sent automatically. Disposition mode can reveal whether the user acknowledges MDNs manually or automatically, and returning manual-action/MDN-sent-manually hides that. The Reporting-UA field can add to fingerprinting.

MDNs do not provide non-repudiation. They cannot be relied on as a guarantee that a message was or was not seen, since they may be lost or bypassed. Finally, a false Disposition-Notification-To address can aim a flood of MDNs at a victim, and because an MDN can include the full message it can be larger than the message that caused it, enabling bandwidth amplification. Hence the rule against automatic sending when addresses differ.
sections.plainLanguage: A reply saying 'I opened it' could be faked, and it tells the sender when and how you read your mail. So you get to decide whether to send one at all.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 3798
sections.content:
Appendix A lists what changed from RFC 3798. The notable points are stronger requirements to get user consent in order to protect privacy, and registration policy changes: the 'Specification Required' policy now matches what IANA already used, and 'X-' prefixed fields are no longer reserved for experimental use.

Several fixes were made to the grammar. The disposition types dispatched and processed had been lost from the ABNF (Erratum #691), and the unused warning-field and failure-field were removed. The ABNF now shows where folding whitespace is allowed, the comparison of Disposition-Notification-To against Return-Path was clarified, and the recommendation to include the MUA's DNS host name in Reporting-UA was removed. The discussion of source routes was dropped as a deprecated email feature.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the list of fixes since the older version: stronger privacy promises, a few mistakes corrected, and some old ideas removed.

items.label: Displayed
items.desc: Shown to someone reading the mailbox; no guarantee it was read or understood.

items.desc: Sent somewhere, for example printed, faxed or forwarded, without necessarily being displayed.

items.label: Processed
items.desc: Handled by rules or a server without being displayed.

items.label: Deleted
items.desc: Deleted; the recipient may or may not have seen it.

Original-Recipient: rfc822;Joe_Recipient@example.com
Final-Recipient: rfc822;Joe_Recipient@example.com
Original-Message-ID: <199509192301.23456@example.org>
Disposition: manual-action/MDN-sent-manually; displayed
